nameStory: The 'variable' in Variable Vertigo refers to how this tiny snail's shell can look quite different from one individual to another, with variations in size, shape, and even the number of 'teeth' (small ridges) inside the shell opening. The genus name Vertigo comes from the Latin word for 'whirlpool' or 'spinning,' describing the way these snails' shells spiral around like a tiny tornado frozen in time.
description: The Variable Vertigo is one of New England's tiniest land snails, so small you could easily mistake it for a grain of rice or a seed. This air-breathing snail carries a brown, cone-shaped shell that spirals upward in tight whorls, creating a miniature tower that's typically less than 3 millimeters tall. Unlike their aquatic cousins, these little gastropods live entirely on land, crawling through leaf litter and soil with their soft, slimy foot. They're part of the whorl snail family, named for their distinctively coiled shells.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Look for a tiny, elongated cone that spirals upward like a miniature ice cream cone, with the point at the top and opening at the bottom

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Incredibly small - about the size of a grain of rice or small seed, easily overlooked among leaf litter

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell ranges from light brown to darker brown, often with a slightly glossy surface when alive

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: The aperture (opening) may have small tooth-like ridges inside, though these vary between individuals and require magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Shell feels smooth and hard to the touch, unlike soft seeds or plant matter it might be confused with

habitat: Variable Vertigo snails live in moist environments with rich organic matter, typically found under logs, in leaf litter, or among moss in deciduous and mixed forests. They prefer areas with good moisture retention but not waterlogged conditions, often near streams or in low-lying areas where humidity stays high. Look for them in the upper layers of decomposing leaves and organic debris.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm and moisture increases from snowmelt, though still quite secretive and requiring careful searching through damp leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods and after rain showers, when they may venture slightly higher in the leaf litter to feed on microscopic fungi and organic matter.
seasonality.fall: Still active in the warming leaf litter, potentially easier to spot as they prepare for winter dormancy and vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and buried deep in leaf litter or soil, essentially impossible to find without disturbing their winter refuges.

funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, Variable Vertigo snails are actually sophisticated recyclers - they help break down dead leaves by eating the microscopic fungi that decompose organic matter, essentially farming their food by encouraging the very process that creates their habitat.
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for seeds, tiny pieces of bark, or other organic debris due to their incredibly small size and brown color. The key difference is that snail shells feel hard and smooth, while seeds often have texture or ridges, and plant debris tends to be more irregular in shape. If you're unsure, gently touch it - a living snail will eventually retreat into its shell or extend its soft body.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, the Variable Vertigo is extremely rare in our region, making any sighting scientifically valuable. This species is much more common in western North America, so finding one here would be quite remarkable and worth reporting to local naturalist groups or museums.
compareHints: Variable Vertigo differs from other Vertigo species mainly in the variable nature of its shell features - while related species like Five-tooth Vertigo have a consistent number of teeth in the shell opening, Variable Vertigo can have anywhere from few to several teeth. It's generally slightly larger than the Delicate Vertigo and has a more elongated shell shape compared to the more rounded Grassland Whorl Snail.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Grassland Whorl Snail differs from other Vertigo species primarily by its habitat preference and shell shape details.
The Delicate Vertigo is distinguished from other Vertigo species by its extremely fragile, translucent shell that's more delicate than its relatives.

Compared to its Vertigo relatives in New England, the Five-tooth Vertigo is distinguished primarily by having exactly five teeth in its shell opening, while the Grassland Whorl Snail has fewer teeth and prefers more open habitats.
